title: This GPU Shouldn't Be This Fast for the Money
creator: Marcus Feld
description:
Full review of the new mid-range card: twelve games at 1440p, power draw, thermals, noise, and how it compares to last year's cards.

The card was a review sample from the manufacturer and is being returned. They had no input on this video and did not see it before publishing.

Test system: 8-core CPU, 32 GB RAM, same drivers for all cards.

sentences.t: So this is the new Radeon card, the one that's supposed to sit right in the middle of the market.
And I've had it on my test bench for about a week now.
Spoiler, it's a lot faster than I expected for the price, but there are a couple of catches.
First, the boring but important bit.
AMD sent me this card as a review sample, and it's going back to them after this video.
They didn't pay me anything, they didn't get to see this video before it went up, and they don't know what I'm about to say.
I've also had sponsorships from hardware brands in the past, but this isn't one, and there's no affiliate link to this card anywhere in the description.
Okay, let's actually look at it.
The card itself is pretty compact, two slots, two fans, and it uses a normal eight-pin power connector.
No weird adapters, which I really appreciate.
The build quality feels fine, a bit plasticky on the shroud, but nothing creaks.
Now, performance.
I tested twelve games at fourteen-forty p, with the same settings I use for every card.
In the big open world games, it's sitting right around sixty to seventy frames a second on high settings.
In competitive shooters, you're well over a hundred and fifty.
And compared to last year's card at this price, it's about twenty five percent faster on average.
That's a proper generational jump, which we haven't really seen in this price range for a while.
But here's catch number one.
Ray tracing.
Turn it on in the heavy games, and the frame rate basically halves.
In one game it dropped from sixty-eight to thirty-one, which is not a nice experience at all.
If ray tracing is the reason you're upgrading, this probably isn't the card for you.
Catch number two is drivers.
I had one game that crashed twice on launch with the first driver, and then a hotfix came out on day four and fixed it.
So it's sorted now, but if you buy one on launch day, update your drivers before you do anything else.
Let's talk power and thermals.
Under a full gaming load, the card pulls about two hundred watts.
The hottest it got was seventy-two degrees, in a case with decent airflow.
And it's quiet, like, genuinely quiet.
I had to put my microphone right next to it to even hear the fans over the room.
So, should you buy it?
If you're on a card from three or four years ago and you mostly play at fourteen-forty p without ray tracing, this is a really good upgrade for the money.
If you care a lot about ray tracing, or you play at 4K, you'll want to spend more.
And if the price creeps up after launch, which it sometimes does, the value argument gets a lot weaker.
I'll be testing it in a small form factor build next week, so if you want to see how it does in a tiny case, stick around.
Thanks for watching.
